metadata.note: The Maine Central's Mountain Division, built by the Portland and Ogdensburg Railroad and completed through Crawford Notch in 1875, was the railroad that opened the eastern White Mountains (Conway, North Conway, Bartlett) to tourism from Portland -- a gap in this map's New Hampshire coverage before now, distinct from the Boston, Concord and Montreal Railroad's approach to the White Mountains from the south/west (see boston_concord_montreal_railroad.geojson). The 131-mile line ran Portland, ME through Fryeburg, Conway, North Conway, Bartlett, and the Crawford Notch pass, then west through Fabyan (crossing the Boston and Maine's Cog Railway branch), Twin Mountain, and Whitefield, across the Connecticut River valley to St. Johnsbury, VT. Leased to the Maine Central in 1888. Passenger service ended in April 1958 and the line was abandoned in 1983; the Conway Scenic Railroad has run heritage excursions on the surviving section from North Conway through Crawford Notch to Fabyan since 1995. Geometry is real-traced from OpenStreetMap (active rail combined with abandoned/disused railway tagging); three out-and-back detours the original pull did not report were removed on 2026-10-20 (see geometry_quality).
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_Division (full station list with mileposts, Portland MP0 to St. Johnsbury MP131.4, via Fryeburg, Conway Center, North Conway, Bartlett, Notchland/Bemis, Crawford Notch, Fabyan, Twin Mountain, Whitefield, Lunenburg VT, Concord VT; line abandoned 1983)

metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.
metadata.maine_central_fixes: 2026-10-20: (1) passenger era ended at 1958, from 1983 - the 1958-1983 years were freight only (Rule 1); (2) the 1875-1888 Portland and Ogdensburg era split out as its own feature in the P&O colour already used in lamoille_valley_railroad.geojson (Rule 4); (3) Conway Scenic Railroad Notch Train added as a tourist_rail feature 1995-2026; (4) three out-and-back routing detours removed from the 2026-08-24 trace, bringing it from 150.9 mi to the documented 131.4 mi, and geometry_quality added. The 1958-1995 gap is intentionally empty.

segments.note: The Portland and Ogdensburg Railroad, chartered 1867, completed its dramatic crossing of the White Mountains at Crawford Notch in 1875, transforming the local economy and opening the White Mountains to Portland-based tourist traffic. At Fabyan the P&O crossed the Boston and Maine's branch to the Mount Washington Cog Railway's Marshfield base (see mount_washington_cog_railway.geojson). Run by the Portland and Ogdensburg (reorganised as the Portland and Ogdensburg Railway in 1886) until the Maine Central lease of 1888, which starts the Maine Central feature; drawn to 1887 so the two eras do not overlap. Split out of the Maine Central feature on 2026-10-20 under Rule 4 - it had been drawn in Maine Central colour for years before the lease. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap on 2026-08-24 (active rail plus abandoned/disused railway tagging, Dijkstra between geocoded stations). On 2026-10-20 three out-and-back detours left by routing to off-line station points were cut out: 2.5 km each way down the B&M Conway Branch to the North Conway station, about 6 km each way at Fabyan, and about 7 km each way near Whitefield (623 -> 526 vertices). The trace now measures 131.4 mi against the documented 131.4 mi Portland - St. Johnsbury (Wikipedia milepost table). No straight-line approximation is known, but the trace is sparse (one vertex per 0.25 mi on average). The three longest hops between Intervale and Bartlett (2.1, 3.1 and 1.1 mi) were checked against a fresh OSM trace and lie within 5 m of the track; the longest hop elsewhere, 3.6 mi near Steep Falls, has not been checked. The alignment drawn is the corridor as it survives today; no relocation between 1875 and 1958 has been checked. Also unchecked for this era: whether the St. Johnsbury - Lunenburg end was the P&O's own line or the separate P&O Vermont Division (see lamoille_valley_railroad.geojson); the full Portland - St. Johnsbury geometry is drawn.

segments.note: Maine Central era, including the B&M-jointly-marketed White Mountains tourist trade. By the 1930s service was down to a single daily round trip Portland - St. Johnsbury (Wikipedia), so the 240-minute headway estimate overstates the later years. Passenger service ended in April 1958 (Wikipedia, Mountain Division; upper_coos_railroad.geojson gives the last trains as 26 Apr 1958, a day not yet confirmed here). Freight continued until the line was abandoned in 1983 - context only, not drawn (Rule 1). The 1919 break between segments was inherited from the original pull and is not explained by any source. Frequency estimated, unsourced.
sources: Segment-level: end year only. The April 1958 end of passenger service is from Wikipedia's Mountain Division article, checked 2026-10-20; the 26 Apr day is from upper_coos_railroad.geojson and is unconfirmed. A MaineDOT Mountain Division study also gives April 1958 but could not be retrieved to re-check. The 1919 start and the headway are NOT sourced.

properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced 2026-10-20 from OpenStreetMap (Overpass, mail.ru mirror): 0.9 mi on the 'Conway Branch' (operator Conway Scenic Railroad) from North Conway station to its junction with the 'Mountain Division' at 44.0657 N, -71.1312, then 28.6 mi on the 'Mountain Division' to Fabyan, shortest path on railway=rail ways excluding yards and sidings. 726 points, 29.5 mi in total; longest gap between consecutive OSM nodes 0.29 mi; no straight-line legs. Check against Wikipedia's Mountain Division mileposts (Intervale Junction 61.4, Crawford Notch 85, Fabyan 88.3): the trace measures 24.3 mi to Crawford Notch (table 23.6) and 28.6 mi to Fabyan (table 26.9), about 6% long. Part of that may be that the OSM junction lies about 2 mi south of the historical Intervale Junction milepost; not resolved. Fabyan end snapped 44 m from the station site. This is the surviving Maine Central alignment, which is also the alignment Conway Scenic runs on.

segments.note: Conway Scenic Railroad excursions from North Conway over the state-owned former Maine Central Mountain Division through Crawford Notch, since 1995 (Conway Scenic's own history). Wikipedia's infobox gives 1994 instead, uncited - conflict recorded, drawn from the railroad's own date. Conway Scenic began in 1974 on the B&M Conway Branch south of North Conway; that operation is not drawn here. Trains are seasonal (summer and fall); headway_min 1440, one round trip a day, is an estimate. Whether every season since 1995 reached Fabyan, rather than turning at Crawford Notch, is not sourced, and seasons that did not run (if any) have not been checked.
sources: Segment-level: the 1995 start is from Conway Scenic's own history page; the 1994 conflict and the North Conway - Crawford Notch - Fabyan extent are from Wikipedia, both checked 2026-10-20. The headway is NOT sourced.
